title: One token looks at three tokens

steps.say: Three tokens 'The cat sat' each become a vector of 4 numbers. Stacked, they form X, a 3 x 4 matrix.
Each token is multiplied by three learned 4 x 4 matrices (Wq, Wk, Wv). Q is what a token looks for, K is what it offers, V is what it passes on.
Every Q row is compared with every K row using a dot product. That gives a 3 x 3 table. For 'sat' the raw scores are [4, 2, 6].
Scores are divided by the square root of 4, which is 2, so numbers stay small. 'sat' row becomes [2, 1, 3].
Softmax turns scores into weights: e^2, e^1, e^3 give [0.25, 0.09, 0.66]. 'sat' pays 66% of its attention to itself and 25% to 'The'.
The weights mix the V rows: new 'sat' = 0.25*V(The) + 0.09*V(cat) + 0.66*V(sat). Each token now carries information from the others.
The cost: the score table is N x N. At 4,096 tokens that is 16.7 million scores per head, per layer. Doubling the text makes it 4 times bigger.

add.label: Cost: N x N table. 4,096 tokens = 16.7M scores per head

title: Why we keep a KV cache

actors.label: Memory
actors.sub: cache = keys and values of past tokens

steps.say: A prompt of 4 tokens enters the model. This first pass is called prefill.
For every token and every layer, the model computes a key (K) and a value (V). We store them in GPU memory: the KV cache.
Without a cache, making token 5 means running all 4 old tokens again plus the new one: 5 units of work. At token 1,000 it is 1,000 units. Wasteful.
With the cache, only the new token goes through the model. Its query reads the old K and V from memory. 1 unit of work.
The new token's own K and V are appended to the cache. The cache grows by one entry every step.
The price is memory. A 7B model with 32 layers needs about 0.5 MB per token. A 4,096-token chat holds 2 GB of cache.
With 20 users at 4,096 tokens each, the cache is 40 GB. The cache, not the weights, is what fills the GPU and limits how many users fit.
Toy GPU: 12 blocks, 16 tokens each. Old method: each request reserves space for its maximum length, in one continuous piece. Request A reserves 6 blocks (96 tokens).
A has only written 20 tokens, so blocks b0-b1 are used. b2-b5 sit empty but nobody else may touch them. B does the same with b6-b11 and uses 2 blocks.
Request C needs just 2 blocks. There are 8 empty blocks, but none are free to take. C must wait. 8 of 12 blocks (67%) are wasted. This is memory fragmentation.
PagedAttention instead cuts the cache into small fixed blocks and hands them out only when a sequence needs them. All blocks start free.
A has 20 tokens: block b0 (16) and b1 (4). B has 30 tokens: b2 (16) and b3 (14). Each request keeps a small table of its blocks.
C arrives and takes b4 and b5 straight away. Only unused slots inside each last block are wasted: 12 + 2 + about 10 tokens, under 5% of memory.
A finishes and frees b0 and b1. New request D gets b6 and b0. Its blocks are not side by side, and that is fine: the table maps them.
Result: almost no wasted memory, so about 2-4 times more requests fit at once. The cost is a small lookup per block in the attention kernel.
Static batching: 4 requests start together. They need 20, 100, 30 and 60 output tokens. The batch cannot finish until the longest is done.
At step 20, R1 is finished. Its slot sits idle for 80 more steps. R5 is waiting in the queue but is not allowed in.
R3 stops at step 30 and R4 at step 60. Both slots go idle. At the end only R2 is working: 1 of 4 slots busy.
Real work was 20+100+30+60 = 210 slot-steps out of 400. The GPU was 52% busy, and R5 to R7 waited 100 steps.
Continuous batching decides at every token step. R1 ends at step 20, and R5 (40 tokens) takes its slot in the very next step.
R3 ends at step 30, so R6 (25 tokens) joins its slot. Nobody waits for the longest request any more.
R4 ends at step 60 and R7 takes over. All 4 slots stay full, GPU is about 95% busy, and throughput in this toy is about 2 times higher.
The cost: every new request needs KV-cache memory right now, and its long prefill can slow the others for one step. This is why paging and chunked prefill go with it.
Text so far: 'Capital of France is'. The small draft model guesses the next 4 tokens fast: ' Paris', ',', ' a', ' city'. Cost: 4 x 5 ms = 20 ms.
All 4 guesses go to the big model together. It checks them in one pass of 40 ms, about the cost of making a single token.
Check 1: big model also wanted ' Paris' (p=0.92). Accept. Check 2: it also wanted ',' (p=0.88). Accept.
Check 3: the big model prefers ' the' and gives ' a' only 2% against the draft's 30%. Reject. Token 4 was built on a bad guess, so it is thrown away too.
The two accepted tokens move to the output. The rejected draft work (2 tokens) is wasted.
The big model already computed what comes at position 3, so it adds its own token ' the' for free. One pass gave 3 new tokens.
Time: plain decoding needs 3 x 40 = 120 ms for 3 tokens. This round took 20 + 40 = 60 ms, 2 times faster, and the text is exactly what the big model would write.
Bad case: if the first guess is wrong, the round gives 1 token for 60 ms, slower than the plain 40 ms. Speed-up depends on how often the draft agrees.

nt.label: Time
nt.sub: first guess wrong: 60 ms for 1 token

groups.label: Time: one cell per GPU step

steps.say: 3 users are chatting. The GPU runs one step every 30 ms, and each step gives each user 1 new token. Smooth.
Now someone sends an 8,000-token document. The GPU must read all of it (prefill) before the first answer word.
Naive plan: do the whole prefill in one step. That step takes about 800 ms. The 3 users get no token for 800 ms, 27 times longer than normal.
Chunked prefill: cut the prompt into 16 chunks of 512 tokens. Each step handles one chunk plus the 3 users' decode tokens, about 45 ms.
The cost: the long prompt itself now needs 16 x 45 = 720 ms to finish, and others are 15 ms slower per token. A fair trade for no 800 ms freezes.
Disaggregated serving goes further: a separate Prefill GPU reads prompts, and the Decode GPU only generates. Prompts can no longer disturb decoding at all.
The price is a transfer: the prompt's KV cache (about 4 GB) must cross the network to the Decode GPU. At 50 GB/s that is 80 ms, plus the cost of 2 pools of GPUs.

actors.label: Prompt = [system prompt 2,000 tokens][question]. Cache matches from the first token, in blocks.

steps.say: Request 1 has a 2,000-token system prompt plus a 50-token question. The cache looks up the hash of the first block.
Nothing is cached, so the model must prefill all 2,050 tokens. That takes about 410 ms before the first word.
The key and value tensors of the 2,000-token prefix are saved (about 1 GB for a 7B model), keyed by the hash of those tokens.
Request 2 has the same system prompt and a new 60-token question. The hash of the prefix matches.
The model reuses the saved 2,000 tokens and prefills only the 60 new ones: about 15 ms instead of 410 ms. 97% of the work is skipped, and cached input tokens are billed much cheaper.
Failure: Request 3 starts with 'Time: 10:41:07' and then the same system prompt. The very first block differs, so the hash never matches.
Fix: put stable text first (system prompt, tools, examples) and changing text last (time, user data, question). Also entries expire after about 5 minutes without use.

actors.label: Running max m and sum l (per row)

steps.say: Standard attention: load Q and K from slow HBM, compute the whole score table S = Q x K^T, and write it back. For 4,096 tokens, S is 4,096 x 4,096 x 2 bytes = 33.5 MB per head.
Softmax reads S back and writes another 33.5 MB table P. Then P and V are read to make the output. About 4 trips of 33.5 MB for each head. The GPU spends its time waiting for memory, not computing.
FlashAttention works on tiles. A block of 128 Q rows is loaded into fast on-chip SRAM, which is about 10 times faster than HBM but tiny.
Take K/V block 1 (128 tokens). Compute a small 128 x 128 score tile inside SRAM. Keep for each row the running max m = 2.0 and running sum l = 4.5.

st.label: Running max m and sum l (per row)

steps.say: K/V block 2 arrives with a bigger score: new max 3.0. Old sum is rescaled by e^(2.0-3.0) = 0.37, so l = 4.5 x 0.37 + 3.2 = 4.9. Softmax is fixed on the fly, no full table needed.

st.label: Running max m and sum l (per row)

steps.say: After the last block, the finished output rows are written to HBM once. S and P were never stored. Memory traffic falls from N x N to N x d, and the answer is exactly the same.

st.label: Running max m and sum l (per row)

steps.say: Result: attention runs about 2 to 4 times faster, and memory grows with N, not N squared. The cost: a harder kernel, and the backward pass recomputes tiles instead of reading them.
A tiny network: input x = 2, h = x * w1, output y = h * w2, loss L = (y - target)^2. Weights w1 = 3 and w2 = 0.5, target = 1.
Forward pass, layer 1: h = 2 * 3 = 6.
Forward pass, layer 2: y = 6 * 0.5 = 3.
Loss = (3 - 1)^2 = 4. We want this smaller. Which weight should change, and by how much?
Backward pass starts at the loss. dL/dy = 2 * (y - target) = 2 * 2 = 4: raising y by 1 raises the loss by about 4.
Chain rule at layer 2. For w2: dL/dw2 = dL/dy * h = 4 * 6 = 24. For h: dL/dh = dL/dy * w2 = 4 * 0.5 = 2.
Chain rule at layer 1. For w1: dL/dw1 = dL/dh * x = 2 * 2 = 4. One backward sweep gave every weight's gradient.
Update with learning rate 0.01: w2 = 0.5 - 0.01*24 = 0.26 and w1 = 3 - 0.01*4 = 2.96. The big gradient moved w2 the most.
Check: y = 2 * 2.96 * 0.26 = 1.54 and loss = (1.54 - 1)^2 = 0.29, down from 4. One step cut the loss by 93%.
The failure case: in a deep net each layer multiplies the gradient by a small number (a sigmoid slope is at most 0.25). After 10 layers, 0.25^10 is about 0.000001, so early layers barely learn.

title: Walking downhill on a loss curve

steps.say: The loss is L = (w - 3)^2. The best weight is w = 3. We start at w = 0, where the loss is 9 and the slope 2*(w - 3) is -6.
Learning rate 0.1: step = -0.1 * slope = +0.6, so w moves to 0.6. Loss falls from 9 to 5.76. Slope is now -4.8.
Next step is 0.48, so w = 1.08, loss 3.69. Steps get smaller by themselves because the slope is flatter near the bottom.
After 20 steps, w = 2.97 and loss is 0.001. Done. Each step gets 20% closer to w = 3.
Failure 1, learning rate too big. Restart at w = 0 with rate 1.05.
Step = -1.05 * -6 = +6.3. We jump past the bottom to w = 6.3, and the loss grows from 9 to 10.9.
Slope is now +6.6, so we jump back to w = -0.63, loss 13.2. Each jump is bigger than the last.
Next w = 6.99 and loss 15.9. The loss keeps growing: training has diverged. Fix: lower the rate, or use Adam, which scales each step.
Failure 2, rate too small. With rate 0.001, each step moves w by only 0.2% of the gap. After 1,000 steps it has covered just 86% of the distance. Safe but slow.

actors.label: Each GPU: 400 MB gradient = 4 chunks of 100 MB

steps.say: 4 GPUs each computed their own gradient: 400 MB, cut into 4 chunks of 100 MB. We follow chunk A, whose values are 1, 2, 3, 4. Goal: everyone gets the sum, 10.
Reduce-scatter, step 1: GPU 0 sends its A=1 to GPU 1, which adds its own: 1 + 2 = 3. At the same time every GPU forwards a different chunk, so all links work.
Step 2: GPU 1 sends 3 to GPU 2: 3 + 3 = 6.
Step 3: GPU 2 sends 6 to GPU 3: 6 + 4 = 10. GPU 3 now holds the full sum of chunk A. (GPUs 0, 1, 2 each finished a different chunk in the same 3 steps.)
All-gather, step 1: finished chunks are passed around the ring. GPU 3 sends A=10 to GPU 0.
Step 2: GPU 0 passes A=10 to GPU 1.
Step 3: GPU 1 passes A=10 to GPU 2. All 4 GPUs have the same sum, so they can all update their weights the same way.
Cost: 6 steps, each GPU sends 100 MB per step = 600 MB total. That is the same for 4 or 400 GPUs. At 50 GB/s a step is 2 ms, so 12 ms in all.

nt.label: 6 steps x 100 MB = 600 MB per GPU; 12 ms at 50 GB/s

steps.say: Failure: GPU 2's link is slow (12.5 GB/s). Every step waits for the slowest sender, so a step takes 8 ms, not 2 ms. The whole all-reduce is 48 ms, 4 times longer, and all GPUs idle.

nt.label: Straggler: 6 steps x 8 ms = 48 ms for everyone

steps.say: Data parallel: every GPU holds a full copy of the model (7B params in fp16 = 14 GB). The batch of 64 samples is split, 32 per GPU.
Each GPU runs forward and backward on its own 32 samples. The two gradients are different.
They average gradients with an all-reduce: (g0 + g1) / 2. Both GPUs apply the same update, so the copies stay identical. Cost: 14 GB of gradients move every step.
Limit: each GPU needs the whole model. A 70B model is 140 GB and does not fit on an 80 GB GPU. Then we split the model itself: tensor parallel.
Tensor parallel: one layer's weight matrix, 8192 x 8192, is cut by columns. GPU 0 gets columns 0-4095 and GPU 1 gets 4096-8191. Each stores half.
Both GPUs receive the same input x and each computes half of the output: y[:, 0:4096] on GPU 0 and y[:, 4096:8192] on GPU 1. Compute is split in two.

The halves must be joined before the next layer. This happens in every layer, about 2 times each, so an 80-layer model needs 160 joins per token. It only works on fast links like NVLink (900 GB/s), not across the network.
Pipeline parallel: an 80-layer model is cut into 4 stages on 4 GPUs, 20 layers each. A batch must pass through stage 1, 2, 3, 4 in order.
If the whole batch goes through as one piece, only one stage works at a time. The other 3 GPUs idle: 25% busy.
Fix: cut the batch into 4 micro-batches m1 to m4 and send them one after another.
Tick 1: m1 enters stage 1. Others wait.
Tick 2: m1 moves to stage 2 and m2 enters stage 1. Two stages work.
Tick 3: m1 is at stage 3, m2 at stage 2, m3 at stage 1. Three busy.
Tick 4: m1 at stage 4, m4 enters stage 1. All 4 GPUs are busy at the same time.
Tick 5: m1 is done. Stage 1 has nothing left to do and goes idle. The ramp-up and ramp-down are the pipeline bubble.
Total 7 ticks, each stage works 4 of them, so 3 of 7 (43%) is wasted. With 16 micro-batches it is 3 of 19 (16%). Cost: more micro-batches means smaller matrices and extra memory for activations.
Instead of one big feed-forward block, a mixture-of-experts layer has 8 smaller ones (E0 to E7). The token 'Paris' arrives at a small router.
The router scores all 8 experts and keeps the top 2: E3 with 0.55 and E6 with 0.30. The other 6 get nothing.
Only E3 and E6 compute. Their outputs are mixed with weights 0.55/0.85 = 0.65 and 0.30/0.85 = 0.35. Work for this token is 2/8 of a dense layer.
The next token, 'def' (code), goes to different experts: E1 and E6. Experts end up specialising in kinds of text.
The memory cost: all 8 experts must sit in GPU memory. Mixtral 8x7B stores 47B parameters but uses only 13B per token. Fast per token, but heavy to store.
The failure: the router may send most tokens to the same expert. If 60% of 1,000 tokens pick E3, E3 gets 600 jobs while the others get about 57 each. The batch waits for E3.
Fixes: a balancing loss during training, and a capacity limit (avg 250 per expert x 1.25 = 312). The 288 extra tokens for E3 are dropped for this layer and just skip it. Quality slips a little.
A query q and a key k are pairs of numbers (a real model has many pairs). Both are [1, 0]. Their dot product is 1.0 and says nothing about where the words are.
RoPE rotates each pair by an angle = position x 30 degrees (toy value). k at position 3 turns 90 degrees: [1, 0] becomes [0, 1].
q at position 5 turns 150 degrees: [-0.87, 0.5].
Dot product: (-0.87 x 0) + (0.5 x 1) = 0.5. That equals cos(60 degrees), and 60 degrees is just the 2 positions between them times 30.
Move both tokens 100 places away: q at 105 (3150 deg = 270 deg, [0, -1]) and k at 103 (210 deg, [-0.87, -0.5]). The vectors are different, but the dot product is 0 + 0.5 = 0.5 again.
So the score depends only on the distance between tokens, not on where they sit. No position table is needed, and the model can compare tokens near or far.

Failure: the model only ever saw angles for positions up to 4,096. At position 32,000 the angles are new and attention scores become noise. Fix: position interpolation, using pos x 4096/32768 = pos / 8.

nt.label: Position 32,000 is outside training range: quality drops

steps.say: With interpolation, position 32,000 is treated as 4,000, inside the trained range. The cost: neighbours are 8 times closer in angle, so fine detail blurs unless the model is fine-tuned a little.

nt.label: Squeeze positions by 8 so they stay inside 4,096

steps.say: User asks: 'What is the population of Paris divided by 3?' The LLM cannot know this reliably, but it can use tools. The loop is Thought, Action, Observation.
Thought: 'I need the population first.' Action: search('population of Paris'). The LLM writes the call as text; the program runs it.
Observation: the tool returns '2.1 million'. This text is added to the context, which grows to 310 tokens.
The LLM reads the whole history again. Thought: 'now divide by 3.' Action: calculator(2100000 / 3).
Observation: 700000. Context is now 480 tokens, and the LLM must read all 480 again for the next turn.
Thought: 'I have what I need.' The LLM writes a final answer instead of an action, and the loop stops.
Failure: the search tool is down and returns nothing. The LLM does not learn from it and repeats the same call again and again. Each lost call still adds text to the context.

Cost: every turn re-reads the full history, so token use grows about with the square of the turns. 8 turns at 100 new tokens each read 3,600 tokens in total. So agents get a hard step limit, like 8 turns, and then stop with an error.
Offline: the company manual (2 million tokens) is cut into chunks of 500 tokens with 50 tokens of overlap. That gives about 4,000 chunks.
Each chunk goes through an embedding model and becomes 768 numbers. Chunks about similar things get similar numbers. They are stored in the vector database.
Online: a user asks 'What is the refund window for annual plans?' The same embedding model turns it into 768 numbers.
The database finds the closest chunks by cosine similarity: chunk 812 scores 0.83, chunk 77 scores 0.79, chunk 2301 scores 0.52. We keep the top 3.
The prompt is the question plus the 3 chunks (about 1,500 tokens). The LLM is told: answer only from these.
The LLM answers 'Annual plans can be refunded within 30 days' and cites chunk 812. The answer is grounded in text we can check.
Failure: in the manual the rule was split: chunk 812 says 'within 30 days' and chunk 813 says 'except annual plans: 14 days'. 813 scored only 0.41, below the top 3, so it was never retrieved.
The LLM sounds confident because it never saw the exception. Fixes: more overlap, search by words (BM25) as well as vectors, and rerank the top 20 into the best 3. Each fix adds delay and cost.
A user opens a page. The page has one ad slot, and the exchange has about 100 ms to sell it. It sends a bid request with the site, the audience and a floor price of $1.00 CPM (per 1,000 views).
The exchange forwards the request to 4 bidders at the same time.
Bids come back in CPM: A $6.00, B $4.50, C $3.20, D $2.10. All are above the $1.00 floor, so all are valid.
The highest bid wins: A. In a second-price auction A pays the second-highest bid ($4.50 CPM), not its own $6.00. For this one view that is $0.0045.
Why this is nice: A can bid its true value ($6.00) with no risk of overpaying, so bidding is simple.
Most exchanges now use first price: A pays its own $6.00. That is $1.50 CPM more (33% above the second price) for the same view, so smart bidders 'shade' their bids down, to around $4.80.
Failure: on the next auction C bids $7.00 but its reply takes 140 ms, after the 100 ms deadline. The exchange drops it, and C loses an impression it would have won.
An advertiser has $1,000 for the day. The even plan is $41.67 per hour, or $166.67 for each 4-hour block shown below.
Without pacing the bidder bids on every auction it can win. Traffic is heavy in the morning, so it spends $200, then $350, then $450.
The $1,000 is gone by about 10:00 AM. For the next 14 hours the campaign is invisible, including the 6-10 PM window, when many buyers are online.

Next day with a pacing controller. Every few minutes it compares actual spend with the plan. At 04:00 the plan says $167 but spend is $300, so it is ahead and cuts the share of auctions it joins to p = 0.56.
If spend falls behind, for example in a slow afternoon, the controller raises p back toward 1.0 to catch up. The result is a flat $167 in every block, and the evening is covered.
Failure: overspend. Win notices arrive about 5 seconds late. When $3 is left, 2,000 bids at $4 CPM are already in flight. If all win, they cost 2,000 x $0.004 = $8, which is $5 over budget.
Fix: the controller lowers p toward 0 as the budget runs out and keeps a small reserve. The cost is that a little money may stay unspent at midnight.

actors.label: Rule: if any bit is 0, the item is NOT in the set

steps.say: A Bloom filter is only a row of bits. Here: 16 bits, all 0, and 3 hash functions h1, h2, h3 that turn any word into a bit number from 0 to 15.
Insert 'cat': h1, h2, h3 give bits 1, 6 and 11. Set all three to 1.
Insert 'dog': it hashes to bits 4, 6 and 14. Bit 6 was already 1 from 'cat', and sharing bits is what keeps the filter small.
Query 'emu': hashes give bits 2, 6, 11. Bit 2 is 0, so 'emu' was definitely never added. This answer is always right.

nt.label: emu: bit 2 is 0, so definitely not in the set

steps.say: Query 'fox', never added: hashes give bits 1, 4, 14. All three are 1, because cat and dog set them. The filter says 'maybe present'. This is a false positive.

nt.label: fox: all 3 bits are 1, says maybe. WRONG, never added

steps.say: Why: 5 of 16 bits are set (31%), so a random word hits 3 set bits with chance 0.31^3, about 3%. A real filter with 9.6 bits per item and 7 hashes has about 1% false positives, and never any false negatives.

nt.label: False positive rate is about (set bits / all bits)^3

steps.say: The limits: you cannot delete. Clearing 'cat' would clear bit 6, which 'dog' also needs, and 'dog' would then be reported missing. And when the filter fills up, false positives climb.

nt.label: Delete cat clears bit 6: dog now looks absent

steps.say: Count distinct users without storing them. Hash each id to 6 random bits: the first 2 bits choose one of 4 registers, and the other 4 bits are used to count leading zeros.
User u1 hashes to 10|0010. Register 2. The rest, 0010, has 2 leading zeros, so rank = 3. R2 becomes 3.
User u2 hashes to 00|1000: register 0, no leading zeros, rank 1. R0 becomes 1.
User u3 hashes to 10|0001: register 2, 3 leading zeros, rank 4. R2 keeps the larger value: max(3, 4) = 4. A rank of 4 is rare (1 in 16), and it hints that many users were seen.
u4 = 01|0100 goes to R1 with rank 2. u5 = 11|1100 goes to R3 with rank 1.
u1 comes back. 10|0010 again gives rank 3, which is less than R2's 4, so nothing changes. Repeats never inflate the count.
u6 = 00|0001: register 0, rank 4. R0 becomes 4. Registers are now [4, 2, 4, 1] and we saw 6 different users.
Estimate = 0.532 x 4^2 / (1/16 + 1/4 + 1/16 + 1/2) = 9.7. The truth is 6. With only 4 registers the error is huge: this is the failure case.

Real HyperLogLog uses 16,384 registers (about 12 KB). Error is 1.04 / sqrt(16,384) = 0.8%, for billions of ids. Two servers can merge by taking the max of each register. But you cannot list or delete users.
